## Backyard Worlds: Planet 9
Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 is a NASA-funded citizen science project launched on 15 February 2017. Volunteers look at short animations ("flipbooks") of small patches of sky made from images of NASA's WISE mission taken over several years and search for objects that shift position between frames. It is a collaboration of NASA, UC Berkeley, the American Museum of Natural History, Arizona State University, the Space Telescope Science Institute and Zooniverse.
Sources: jpl-backyard-worlds

## Why motion and why people
Nearby objects appear to move across the sky, while distant ones barely shift, so searching for motion is a systematic way to find nearby objects such as brown dwarfs. Software struggles with image artefacts, especially in crowded star fields: brightness spikes from stars and blurry blobs from light scattered inside the instrument. People recognise real moving objects and ignore the artefacts.
Sources: jpl-backyard-worlds

## From a flag to a result
A volunteer's flag is not a discovery. The science team prioritises flagged objects for follow-up observations by professional astronomers, and participants share credit in resulting publications. By 2024 the project had helped build a census of more than 3,500 objects within 65 light-years of the Sun, published in The Astrophysical Journal with citizen scientists as co-authors.
Sources: jpl-backyard-worlds, nasa-bw-census

## Candidate states in Q-FIT
Q-FIT keeps four states apart. An AI-generated candidate was suggested by software and nobody has looked at it. An unreviewed candidate is waiting for human inspection. A human-reviewed candidate has at least one recorded review by a person. A scientifically confirmed result exists only when an external reference (a publication or a professional follow-up) is recorded. Q-FIT never calls a candidate a discovery, and human reviews enter an evaluation or training dataset only after a separate validation step.
Sources: qfit-spec
